speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. To help me understand your condition, can you describe exactly what happens during these episodes of dizziness and vertigo? Specifically, does the room feel like it is spinning, or do you feel lightheaded and faint?

speaker: Patient
text: 70-year-old woman. The patient presents with sudden episodes of dizziness that are position dependent. She describes experiencing a false sensation of motion and occasional spinning, indicative of vertigo. She denies any recent illnesses, injuries, or significant changes in health status, apart from age-related hearing loss (presbycusis).

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for that description. Do these episodes typically last for less than a minute, or do they persist for longer periods? Additionally, do you experience any ringing in your ears or noticeable hearing changes specifically during the dizzy spells?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Episodes of dizziness and spinning sensation. I also have Position dependent vertigo, No recent illness, No hearing loss besides presbycusis.

speaker: Doctor
text: I see. Does the spinning sensation start immediately when you change your head position, such as rolling over in bed or looking up? Also, have you noticed any imbalance or difficulty walking during these episodes?

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: No significant past medical or surgical history. No history of Meniere's disease, vestibular neuritis, or labyrinthitis. Social history: Retired school teacher. Lives alone. Non-smoker, occasional wine. Enjoys light gardening.

speaker: Doctor
text: Do you experience any nausea or involuntary eye movements (nystagmus) when these dizzy spells occur? Additionally, are you currently taking any medications that might affect your balance or blood pressure?

speaker: Patient
text: Denies headache, tinnitus, hearing loss, nausea, vomiting, or recent respiratory infections.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Positive for right-sided horizontal nystagmus when moving from sitting to supine position, suggestive of BPPV

speaker: Doctor
text:
The positive Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre with nystagmus confirms Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). I will proceed with the Epley maneuver to reposition the displaced otoconia.

DIAGNOSIS READY: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV)
